Mobile health (mHealth) refers to medical and public healthcare practices supported by mobile devices such as smartphones, tablets, and personal digital assistants. These technologies enable the creation, storage, retrieval, and transmission of information between users. 9. mHealth primarily relies on mobile phone functionalities like voice, SMS, and MMS, but also includes advanced applications such as GPS, Bluetooth, and 3G/4G systems. These technologies enhance healthcare delivery by leveraging mobile networks' reach and speed, enabling data capture, processing, and exchange, and transforming the health sector. 10. The effectiveness of mHealth has been reviewed in 17 studies, including 10 Cochrane reviews. These studies vary in the type and purpose of technology, ranging from email for clinical communication to mobile phone reminders for healthcare appointments. 11. Evidence on mHealth effectiveness ranges from negligible or small effects to significant improvements in targeted health behaviors. Common applications include information management, client self-management, clinical decision support, communication, and service delivery. 12. Some healthcare providers appreciate mHealth for improving care coordination by connecting them with peers, higher-level workers, clients, and communities. This is particularly beneficial for lower-level healthcare workers in lowand middle-income countries. 13. Lower-level healthcare providers value the ability to reach higher-level professionals via mHealth, as it improves care quality, health outcomes, and client satisfaction. However, negative responses from higher-level professionals can discourage lower-level providers from seeking support. 14. mHealth technologies are not perceived as supportive when those assigned to provide clinical support via these technologies are unresponsive. This undermines the intended benefits of mHealth interventions. 15. Supervised healthcare providers report that mHealth-facilitated supervision changes their work dynamics, making their activities more visible. While some perceive this as positive, others view it negatively, depending on the context and implementation. 16. Automated text messages about illness management sent to healthcare providers can be helpful, but their effectiveness depends on the content, timing, and relevance of the messages. 17. Many mHealth studies are small-scale or pilot projects, and findings from larger-scale programs may differ due to resource constraints and less intensive management. mHealth technologies are not a universal solution for poorly performing healthcare systems but can enhance primary healthcare delivery in functional systems. 18. More studies from high-income countries are needed to strengthen evidence for findings with low or very low confidence. Policymakers and practitioners should involve healthcare providers in the planning stages of mHealth programs to improve uptake and usage.
